prompt: On a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, star X has a higher surface temperature than star Y, but a lower luminosity. What kind of stars are X and Y?
options: X is a hot but faint star (such as a white dwarf); Y is a cool but very bright star (such as a red giant)
X is a red giant; Y is a white dwarf
X and Y are both main-sequence stars of the same mass
X is a cool dim star; Y is a hot bright star
answer: X is a hot but faint star (such as a white dwarf); Y is a cool but very bright star (such as a red giant)
hint: High temperature with low luminosity puts X at the bottom left; low temperature with high luminosity puts Y at the top right.

prompt: Star Y is a red giant and star X is a white dwarf. Which best describes the fusion occurring in the core of each?
options: In Y (a red giant), helium is fusing into carbon (and heavier elements); in X (a white dwarf) there is essentially no fusion at all
Both stars are fusing hydrogen into helium at the same rate
In Y, hydrogen fuses into helium; in X, carbon fuses into iron
In X, hydrogen fuses into helium; in Y there is no fusion
answer: In Y (a red giant), helium is fusing into carbon (and heavier elements); in X (a white dwarf) there is essentially no fusion at all
hint: A red giant has finished core hydrogen burning and is fusing helium; a white dwarf is the inert remnant left after fusion has ceased.

prompt: Which design feature of a transformer improves its efficiency, and why?
options: The iron core is built from thin insulated laminations, which greatly reduces the eddy currents (and the heat they generate) circulating in the core
The core is made of many separate pieces so magnetic flux can escape between them
The copper wire is made as thin as possible to increase its resistance
The primary and secondary coils are wound on separate cores so they do not interfere
answer: The iron core is built from thin insulated laminations, which greatly reduces the eddy currents (and the heat they generate) circulating in the core
hint: Laminating the core, using thick low-resistance wire, and keeping a continuous closed core for full flux linkage all cut losses.

prompt: The radioactive decay curve for americium-242 shows its mass halving every 16 hours. Calculate the decay constant of Am-242.
hint: $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$ with $t_{1/2} = 16$ h.

prompt: A sample of Am-242 starts with a mass of 80 micrograms and has a decay constant of 0.043 h$^{-1}$. Calculate the time taken for the mass remaining to fall to 8 micrograms.
hint: $8 = 80\,e^{-\lambda t}$, so $t = \dfrac{\ln 10}{\lambda}$.

prompt: A 200 kg rocket coasting away from a planet has a speed of 5500 m s$^{-1}$ at one point and 2900 m s$^{-1}$ at a point further out. Calculate the magnitude of the change in its kinetic energy between the two points.

The 200 kg rocket has speed 5500 m s$^{-1}$ at $R = 4.3 \times 10^{6}$ m from the planet's centre and 2900 m s$^{-1}$ at $R = 2.5 \times 10^{7}$ m. Using conservation of energy, calculate the mass of the planet. Use $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$.
hint: The loss of kinetic energy equals the gain in gravitational potential energy: $\tfrac{1}{2}m(v_1^2 - v_2^2) = GMm\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)$.

prompt: Light of frequency $7.5 \times 10^{14}$ Hz strikes calcium metal, which has a work function of 2.9 eV. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of an emitted photoelectron, in joules. Use $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s and $1$ eV $= 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ J.
hint: $K_{max} = hf - \phi$; convert the work function to joules first.

prompt: A photoelectron leaves the calcium surface with $3.2 \times 10^{-20}$ J of kinetic energy into a uniform electric field of 5.2 N C$^{-1}$ that pushes it back towards the surface. Calculate the maximum distance it travels from the surface. Use electron charge $1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ C.
hint: The field does work $qEd$ bringing it to rest, so $d = \dfrac{K_{max}}{qE}$.

prompt: Red laser light of wavelength 655 nm passes through double slits separated by $5.0 \times 10^{-5}$ m. Calculate the angle between the central bright line and the first-order bright line.
hint: $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ with $m = 1$.

prompt: The 655 nm red laser is replaced with a 520 nm green laser (same slits, same screen). How does the interference pattern change?
options: The bright lines move closer together, because the fringe spacing is proportional to the wavelength
The bright lines move further apart
The pattern is unchanged
The bright lines disappear entirely
answer: The bright lines move closer together, because the fringe spacing is proportional to the wavelength
hint: Shorter wavelength gives a smaller diffraction angle for each order, so the fringes bunch up.

prompt: In Step Y of the CNO cycle, carbon-13 (13.003 u) fuses with a proton (1.007 u) to form nitrogen-14 (14.003 u). Calculate the energy released in this step. Use 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c$^2$.
hint: Mass defect = 13.003 + 1.007 - 14.003 u; multiply by 931.5 MeV/u. (Step X releases only 1.20 MeV, so Step Y loses more mass.)

prompt: An apple is thrown horizontally to the east from the window of a car that is moving with uniform velocity to the north. Ignoring air resistance, which best describes the apple's motion during its flight?
options: Its horizontal velocity is the constant vector sum of the eastward throw and the northward car velocity; its vertical motion is free fall at g, entirely independent of the horizontal motion
The apple travels due east only, since that is the direction it was thrown
The apple's horizontal speed steadily decreases while its vertical speed steadily increases
The northward motion of the car has no effect, so the apple lands due east of the release point
answer: Its horizontal velocity is the constant vector sum of the eastward throw and the northward car velocity; its vertical motion is free fall at g, entirely independent of the horizontal motion
hint: The apple keeps whatever horizontal velocity it had at release (east + north); gravity only acts vertically.

prompt: In a light-clock thought experiment on a train moving at $v = 0.96c$, an observer inside the train measures the light's return trip between two mirrors as 15 nanoseconds. How long does an observer outside the train measure this trip to take?
hint: $t = \dfrac{t_0}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}$ with $t_0 = 15$ ns and $v = 0.96c$.

prompt: An exercise bike uses magnets on either side of a spinning thick aluminium flywheel to make pedalling harder. What is the principle involved?
options: The moving aluminium experiences a changing magnetic flux, which induces eddy currents in it; by Lenz's law these currents oppose the motion, producing a retarding torque
The magnets physically rub against the flywheel, creating friction
The aluminium becomes permanently magnetised and sticks to the magnets
The magnets change the flywheel's mass, making it harder to turn
answer: The moving aluminium experiences a changing magnetic flux, which induces eddy currents in it; by Lenz's law these currents oppose the motion, producing a retarding torque
hint: This is magnetic (eddy-current) braking: no contact, but a real opposing force whenever the wheel moves.

prompt: The rider wants a larger opposing torque on the flywheel. Which adjustment to the magnets would achieve this?
options: Move the magnets closer to the flywheel, so the field through the aluminium is stronger and the rate of change of flux is greater
Move the magnets further from the flywheel
Turn the magnets so their poles face away from the flywheel
Replace the magnets with pieces of unmagnetised iron
answer: Move the magnets closer to the flywheel, so the field through the aluminium is stronger and the rate of change of flux is greater
hint: A stronger field (or stronger magnets) means larger induced eddy currents and a bigger braking torque.

prompt: In a hammer throw, a 7.0 kg projectile rotates in a circle of radius 1.6 m with a period of 0.50 s. It is released at point P where its velocity is directed 45 degrees above the horizontal. Calculate the vertical component of its velocity at P.
hint: Speed in the circle is $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$; the vertical component is $v\sin45^\circ$.

prompt: The hammer is released at point P, 1.2 m above the ground, moving at 45 degrees above the horizontal (so both velocity components are 14.2 m s$^{-1}$). Calculate the horizontal range from P to where it lands. Use $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.
hint: Solve $-1.2 = 14.2\,t - 4.9\,t^2$ for the total flight time, then range $= 14.2\,t$.

prompt: Three charged particles X, Y and Z enter the same uniform magnetic field at the same speed along parallel paths, and follow different curved paths. What determines the differences?
options: The direction each path curves shows the sign of the charge; the radius of each path ($r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$) shows each particle's mass-to-charge ratio (a straight path means the particle is neutral)
Only the mass of each particle matters; charge has no effect
The particles repel each other, which bends their paths
The field strength is different for each particle
answer: The direction each path curves shows the sign of the charge; the radius of each path ($r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$) shows each particle's mass-to-charge ratio (a straight path means the particle is neutral)
hint: Opposite charges curve in opposite directions; a larger mass-to-charge ratio gives a larger radius.

prompt: A capsule of mass $1.2 \times 10^{4}$ kg moves in a circle of radius 200 m around the International Space Station at 0.233 m s$^{-1}$. Calculate the centripetal force required for this circular motion.
hint: $F_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

prompt: Calculate the gravitational force of attraction between the capsule ($1.2 \times 10^{4}$ kg) and the ISS ($4.2 \times 10^{5}$ kg) when their centres are 200 m apart. Use $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$.
hint: $F_G = \dfrac{Gm_1 m_2}{r^2}$.

prompt: The circular motion of the capsule around the ISS can be fully accounted for by the gravitational attraction between the two spacecraft.
options: True
False
hint: The centripetal force needed (about 3.3 N) is roughly a million times larger than the mutual gravitational force (about $8 \times 10^{-6}$ N), so gravity cannot be responsible.
